transcript.text: Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.

Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At that price, buyers can purchase the amount they want and sellers can sell the amount they offer, so there is no pressure for price to change. A demand or supply shift creates a new intersection and can change both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
Find the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
On a graph, use the intersection of the demand and supply curves.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage; a price above equilibrium creates a surplus.
Report both the equilibrium price and the corresponding equilibrium quantity.
A common mistake is to call any intersection or stated price an equilibrium. Equilibrium occurs only where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

Price in dollars is vertical; quantity in thousands is horizontal. Downward demand and upward supply intersect at E, quantity 150 and price 5. No curve shifts are shown. Above 5 supply exceeds demand; below 5 demand exceeds supply.

Demand and supply intersect at a price of $5 and quantity of 150 thousand. Buyers want exactly the amount sellers offer at that point. A price above $5 creates a surplus; a price below $5 creates a shortage. This example finds equilibrium without shifting either curve.
At a price below $5 on this graph, which quantity is larger, and what pressure does that create on price?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.

A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price. Buyers competing for limited supply put upward pressure on price. A surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded; sellers then face pressure to lower price. Adjustment tends toward the price where the two quantities are equal.
At the current price, buyers want 180 units and sellers offer 120 units.
A price above equilibrium creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.
A common mistake is to reverse shortage and price pressure. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward.

The horizontal axis is quantity of gas in thousands of gallons and the vertical axis is price of gas per gallon. D0 slopes downward from price $6 at quantity 0 to quantity 300 thousand at price $0. S0 slopes upward from the origin to price $6 at quantity 300 thousand. The curves intersect at price $3 and quantity 150 thousand. At price $2, quantity demanded is 200 thousand and quantity supplied is 100 thousand. At price $4, quantity demanded is 100 thousand and quantity supplied is 200 thousand.

At a price of $2 per gallon, the graph shows quantity demanded of 200 thousand gallons and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Because buyers want 100 thousand more gallons than sellers offer, the market has a shortage of 200 - 100 = 100 thousand gallons. Upward pressure on price follows.
At a price of $4, buyers want 100 thousand gallons and sellers offer 200 thousand. Calculate the imbalance and predict the pressure on price.
Return to the game and master this concept.
Outcome: Use elasticity to determine and calculate the distribution of tax burdens.

Tax incidence depends on relative elasticity: the less responsive side of the market bears more of the tax burden. That side changes quantity less when the tax alters the price it pays or receives, so more of the tax wedge appears on its side of the market. Legal responsibility for remitting the tax does not determine its economic burden.
The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.
The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden; identify that side from the market conditions.
A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in quantity but a large increase in buyer price.
In one market, demand is much more elastic than supply.
The less elastic side bears more of a tax because it changes quantity less readily. The side that legally sends the payment to government need not bear most of the burden.

Price vertical and quantity horizontal. Demand is P = 35 minus 0.2 Q; supply is P = 5 plus 0.1 Q. Initially quantity 100 and price 15. A 6 dollar tax shifts supply up to P = 11 plus 0.1 Q. New quantity 80, buyer price 19, seller receipt 13. Buyers bear 4 and sellers 2 per unit; demand is less elastic at the initial equilibrium.

Before tax, price is $15 and quantity is 100. A $6 tax reduces quantity to 80; buyers pay $19 and sellers receive $13. Buyers bear $4 per unit, or $320, while sellers bear $2 per unit, or $160. At the initial equilibrium, demand is less elastic than supply, so buyers bear more of the wedge.
When demand is less elastic than supply, which side is less able to avoid the tax?
Return to the game and master this concept.
